The .gitignore file for the mvis-bin package ignores all files by default and then un-ignores a small set of expected AUR metadata files: .nvchecker.toml, .gitignore itself, PKGBUILD, and .SRCINFO. This is a conventional and innocuous configuration for an AUR repository, ensuring that only the relevant packaging files are tracked while build artifacts and unrelated files are excluded. There are no commands, network requests, file modifications, or obfuscated code present. The file contains no executable content and no behavior that could be interpreted as malicious or dangerous. It is purely a standard Git ignore configuration.

The .SRCINFO file is a standard AUR metadata file containing package description, version, source URLs, and checksums. It contains no executable code, network requests, or system modification commands. The file simply defines how the mvis-bin package should be built and sourced from official GitHub releases. All source URLs point to legitimate project locations (https://github.com/SickleFire/m-vis). While there are two sha256sum entries (one appearing twice with slightly different values), this is a metadata inconsistency rather than a security vulnerability. The file does not execute any commands, access local files outside its scope, or attempt to modify system state. It is a benign configuration file typical of AUR packages.

This PKGBUILD file appears safe and follows standard AUR packaging practices. The package fetches its sources (README, LICENSE, and prebuilt binary) directly from the project's official GitHub repository (SickleFire/m-vis) at a specific version tag (v0.6.0). All sources are properly checksummed with sha256sums. The package function performs standard installation operations: installing the binary to `/usr/bin/`, documentation to `/usr/share/doc/`, and license to `/usr/share/licenses/`. There are no obfuscated commands, network exfiltration, or unexpected system modifications. This is a straightforward binary package that downloads from the upstream source and installs it with proper documentation.

The configuration follows standard AUR packaging practices: using GitHub as a source, specifying the upstream repo, enabling latest release checking, and setting a tag prefix. There are no network requests, obfuscated code, dangerous commands (eval/base64/curl/wget), or unexpected file operations. The code is consistent with ordinary packaging workflow and does not exfiltrate data, install backdoors, or execute attacker-controlled code.
